t: Introduction: topic, aim and lecture plan
n: In this lecture we shall consider the development of forensic medicine, the normative foundations of examination, and brain death. The first direction is the history of the development of forensic medicine in the world and in Uzbekistan, and the periods in the formation of the service. The second direction is the normative foundations that govern examination: the Law "On Forensic Examination", the Code of Criminal Procedure and the rights of the expert. The third direction is brain death; death of the cerebral cortex as the beginning of biological death is covered in the chapter on thanatology. Learning aim: to know the definitions of forensic medicine and of examination, the subject of the science and its sections, and to be able to distinguish them.

t: The concept of forensic medicine and forensic medical examination
n: The concept of forensic medicine and forensic medical examination. Forensic medicine is a distinct science that studies medico-biological questions in judicial and investigative activity. Examination is an investigation with a set task, and ends with the drawing up of the expert's conclusion. It has four features: the investigation is carried out by a knowledgeable specialist, on a specific task, usually for evaluation; the procedure is strictly defined; and the process and result are formalised in a document. Attention: forensic medicine is a science, whereas forensic medical examination is the practical application of the science's knowledge. Do not confuse these two concepts.

t: The subject of forensic medicine
n: The subject of forensic medicine. The subject is the theory and practice of forensic medical examination. M. I. Avdeev was the first, in 1948, to propose a scientifically grounded system of the subject. This system rests on forensic medical practice and is closely tied to the objects of examination. The subject consists of 8 sections. The first and second sections are history, and organisational and procedural questions. The third and fourth are external factors and death, and examination of the dead body. The fifth and sixth are living persons and physical evidence. The seventh and eighth are investigation and court materials, and professional offences.

t: Current components of the science
n: Current components of the science. The science now consists of 9 parts: history, foundations, thanatology, traumatology and others. The remaining parts are obstetrics-gynaecology, toxicology, biology, external factors and identification. They are easy to remember in groups: history and law, body and injury, special sections, and other parts. Remember also that in 2002 the section on professional offences separated as the science "Legal foundations of medical practice".

t: Links of forensic medicine with other sciences
n: Links of forensic medicine with other sciences. Forensic medicine is not a fundamental but an applied science; it is linked with the medical, legal, natural and philosophical sciences. The fundamental medical sciences form the foundation, and without them examination cannot be done. From the clinical sciences, traumatology, obstetrics and ophthalmology are needed. Chemistry is needed in toxicology, and physics in the effects of temperature, current and pressure. Philosophy and logic are needed for dialectical evaluation and for logic in the conclusion. The expert cannot know all specialties fully at the same time. The treating specialist approaches from diagnosis and treatment, whereas the expert approaches from the legal evaluation of circumstances.

t: Quick question 1: the science and its composition
n: Now we consolidate what has been covered with quick questions. First question: what is the subject of forensic medicine? Answer: the theory and practice of forensic medical examination; the system was proposed in 1948 by M. I. Avdeev. Second question: which part became a separate science in 2002? Answer: professional offences of medical staff, that is, "Legal foundations of medical practice". Third question: which clinical knowledge is needed in criminal abortion and eye injury? Answer: obstetrics-gynaecology and ophthalmology.

t: Principles of forensic medical examination
n: Principles of forensic medical examination. The law lists the basic principles: legality, respect for human rights and freedoms, independence of the expert, objectivity, comprehensiveness and completeness. These principles are generalised facts drawn from the study and analysis of many years of expert practice. Expert investigation is always scientifically grounded. The independent expert is personally responsible for the investigation, result and conclusion and works only within the limits of his competence. By the right of initiative, the expert may in the conclusion express an opinion also on other questions important for the case, beyond those he was asked.

t: Objects of examination and the period of identification
n: Objects of examination and the period of identification. There are four objects of forensic medical examination: the dead body, living persons, physical evidence, and materials of criminal and civil cases. The objects are presented by the person who ordered the examination, who himself answers for their authenticity. An object can be a source of evidence only during a certain period. For example, most abrasions and bruises are best examined within the first 10–15 days. Attention: there is a risk of error. This period applies to most abrasions and bruises; do not generalise it to all injuries.

t: Methods of forensic medical examination
n: Methods of forensic medical examination. Methods are divided into three groups: general scientific, particular and special. General scientific methods include observation, description, comparison and measurement and are used in different sciences. Particular methods, for example morphological, clinical, radiological and chemical, are characteristic of one science. Special methods include photographic comparison, matching an injury to a knife, and establishing the identity of a person and an instrument. A method must be scientifically grounded, simple, give a stable result and permit repeated investigation. Only methods permitted or recommended by the country's chief forensic medical examination are used.

t: Case analysis 1: a situation on the basics of examination
n: Case analysis: a situation on the basics of examination. An investigator ordered an examination of a body, a living person and a knife. The objects are presented by the person ordering, who answers for their authenticity. The expert uses observation and measurement, which is a general scientific method; radiological and chemical investigation, which is a particular method; and comparative study of the knife, which is a special method. As to timing, abrasions and bruises are best examined within the first 10–15 days; for signs of disease, the body is examined as soon as possible. Attention: a particular method is not the same as a special method; special methods are used mainly in forensic medical practice.

t: World history: the ancient period
n: World history: the ancient period. The laws of Sparta, that is, the "laws of Lycurgus", in the 9th–8th century BC noted medical examination; Hippocrates took part in drawing up the rules. The body of Caesar was inspected by the physician Antistius: of 23 wounds only one led to death. This event dates from 44 BC. In the Code of Justinian, in the 6th century, the conclusion of physicians and midwives was considered more important than a witness's testimony. That is, even in antiquity special weight was given to the medical conclusion as evidence.

t: World history: the Middle Ages and the Renaissance
n: World history: the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. In 1247 in China, Song Ci wrote the "Xi Yuan Lu". Its parts are devoted to the body and injuries, weapons, strangulation and drowning, and poisons. In the 13th century in Bologna, Hugh of Lucca gave opinions before the tribunal. In the 14th century in France there were royal surgeons, and the first inspection took place in Montpellier. In 1532 the "Carolina" in Germany stated that the participation of a physician in cases of murder, suicide and poisoning is necessary. Paré, in the "Opera chirurgica", covered injuries, asphyxia, carbon monoxide and samples of conclusions.

t: Formation of the science and scientists of the 19th–20th centuries
n: Formation of the science and scientists of the 19th–20th centuries. Forensic medicine began to become a separate science at the end of the 16th and beginning of the 17th century. In 1681 I. Schreyer first applied the lung test to the body of a newborn. In I. Bohn's work "Medicina forensis specimen" it was proposed to call the science "forensic medicine"; this name is still used in many countries. At the end of the 18th and beginning of the 19th century, European universities taught the science together with anatomy and surgery, and separate departments were opened later. In 1846 N. I. Pirogov produced an atlas of examination of the body and gave information on gunshot injuries. After the Second World War many textbooks were written.

t: Central Asia: the Sharia period and thinkers
n: Central Asia: the Sharia period and thinkers. Until the beginning of the 20th century, justice on the territory of present-day Uzbekistan was based on the norms of Sharia; the involvement of medical representatives was not provided for. Nevertheless, in the works of Beruni, Ibn Sina and Ismail Jurjani there is information relating to forensic medicine or connected with it. Ibn Sina's "Canon of Medicine" wrote about postmortem changes of the body, certain types of violent death, poisons and injuries. Attention: this information is the result of study not for the administration of justice but mainly for the purpose of giving correct medical help.

t: Quick question 2: history of the world and the East
n: Quick questions: history of the world and the East. First question: which test was first applied in 1681 in Zeitz in examining the body of a newborn? Answer: the lung test, I. Schreyer. Second question: who proposed calling the science "forensic medicine", and in which work? Answer: I. Bohn, "Medicina forensis specimen". Third question: which scientist produced in 1846 an atlas for examination of bodies? Answer: N. I. Pirogov. And from the East, the author of the "Canon of Medicine", Ibn Sina. Remember: Schreyer, lung; Bohn, name; Pirogov, atlas; Ibn Sina, "Canon of Medicine". Link each person to one work or deed.

t: Chronology of forensic medicine departments in Uzbekistan
n: Chronology of forensic medicine departments in Uzbekistan. Scientific research began in the 1920s and is mainly linked with departments of higher medical schools. The sequence of departments is as follows: 1920, Turkestan University; 1935, Samarkand Medical Institute; 1959, Andijan Medical Institute; 1972, Tashkent Paediatric; 1993, a course of advanced training. Markovin, Kolosova, Shahobiddinov, Eydlin and other scientists made a weighty contribution to the development of the science. There are now 9 departments of forensic medicine in higher medical education; the teaching process goes together with scientific and practical work.

t: Case analysis 2: a situation from a historical source
n: Case analysis: a situation from a historical source. Ibn Sina's "Canon of Medicine" gives information on postmortem changes of the body, poisoning and injuries. At the same time, until the beginning of the 20th century in this region, justice was based on the norms of Sharia, and the involvement of medical representatives was not provided for. Attention: the existence of information on forensic medicine does not mean that a forensic medical examination was carried out. The information was obtained mainly in order to give correct medical help. Question: what was the aim of Ibn Sina's information, and why can it not be regarded as an examination carried out for the administration of justice?

t: The expert service in Uzbekistan: four periods
n: The expert service in Uzbekistan: four periods. The service belongs to the health-care system; its main task is to resolve medico-biological questions in the judicial and investigative sphere. Four periods are conventionally distinguished: until the 1920s, until the 1950s, 1950–1991, and from 1991 to the present. In the first period examinations were sporadic. In the second they were carried out on the basis of departments. In the third, the Chief Bureau and territorial bureaus worked. The fourth period begins in 1991: an independent service and new documents. Until 1991 the service relied on the instructions of the health ministry of the former union.

t: First period: the Russian statute and three instances
n: First period: the Russian statute and three instances. The service was subordinate to the Medical Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and the procedure was defined by the statute of 1842. Hospital physicians worked in the first instance; in complex cases higher instances were added. The chain is as follows: the request of an administrative body, then hospital physicians, after them district physicians and chiefs, and finally the physicians of the medical council. This procedure was applied in Turkestan; in 1916–1918 a staff forensic physician, V. S. Elkin, worked in Tashkent.

t: Second and third periods: from departments to bureaus
n: Second and third periods: from departments to bureaus. In the second period, laboratories were opened at departments, and examinations were carried out by teaching staff. In 1945, on the initiative of I. V. Markovin, the Republican Office of Forensic Medical Examination was opened in Tashkent. In the third period, in 1950, the Chief Bureau was formed and bureaus were opened in the regions. The procedure was uniform throughout the union. That is, the service passed from laboratories at departments to a system of independent bureaus.

t: Fourth period: independence and new normative documents
n: Fourth period: independence and new normative documents. The fourth period begins in 1991 and reflects the formation of the forensic medical expert service of an independent state. In a state governed by law, fully, properly and promptly meeting the need of law-enforcement bodies for examination became an urgent task. New normative documents were developed, that is, laws, instructions, rules and standards; the Law "On Forensic Examination" was adopted for the first time. The composition of institutions was improved and new structures were opened; a system for training specialists, advanced training and attestation was created.

t: Case analysis 3: periods in the development of the service
n: Case analysis: periods in the development of the service. Situation: the archive records that in 1945 the "Republican Office of Forensic Medical Examination" was opened in Tashkent; the initiator was Professor I. V. Markovin. To which period does this belong? To the second, that is, until the 1950s; examinations were carried out mainly in departments of medical universities. Compare: in 1950 the Chief Bureau of Forensic Medical Examination of the Ministry of Health was established, which is the third period, 1950–1991. Attention: there is a risk of error. In the fourth period, which began in 1991, an independent service was formed and the Law "On Forensic Examination" was adopted for the first time.

t: Legal terms: law, statute, code
n: Legal terms: law, statute, code. Law is a system of binding rules guaranteed by the state, regulating social relations. A statute is a generally binding normative legal document. Attention: a statute and a code are not the same thing. A code is a systematised collection of statutes in one field. The Criminal Code defines the offence, the limits of liability and punishment. The Code of Criminal Procedure, that is, the CCP, defines the procedure for investigating a criminal case and trying it in court.

t: Article 173 of the CCP: mandatory cases of examination
n: Article 173 of the CCP: mandatory cases of examination. An examination is carried out on the basis of a ruling of the inquiry and investigation bodies or a court order. Under the article, the cause of death and the type and severity of injury are determined. In the sexual sphere, sexual intercourse, pregnancy and abortion are determined. Age is determined if documents are absent or doubtful. The physical condition of the accused, the victim and the witness is also examined. The article also provides for determining the need for and possibility of treatment of venereal and other infectious diseases. An examination is also ordered in other cases that are important for the case and require special knowledge.

t: Place of examination and judicial investigation
n: Place of examination and judicial investigation. An examination may be carried out in the bureau, outside it, or in a mixed way; the person providing the conditions differs. If it is carried out in an institution, the conditions are the responsibility of the head of the institution; if outside, the person ordering is responsible. In the mixed arrangement, part is done in the bureau and part outside, for example exhumation. In judicial investigation the expert takes full part in the sitting, examines the circumstances of the case and has the right to ask questions. The expert reads out the written conclusion at the sitting; the conclusion is attached to the minutes of the sitting.

t: Quick question 3: procedural foundations
n: Quick questions: procedural foundations. First question: in which cases does Article 173 of the CCP make an examination mandatory? Answer: when the cause of death and the nature and severity of bodily injury are determined. Second question: when is an examination ordered to determine age? Answer: if there are no documents on age or the documents raise doubt. Third question: where may an examination be carried out? Answer: in the bureau, outside it, or in a mixed way; in exhumation the body is opened at the cemetery. Attention: the list in Article 173 is not exhaustive; an examination is also ordered in other cases where special knowledge is necessary.

t: The forensic expert: rights and duties
n: The forensic expert: rights and duties. Rights of the expert: to familiarise himself with the case materials, to file a petition, with permission to ask questions, to demand an interpreter, and to appeal. In the conclusion he expresses an opinion also on additional questions important for the case; this is the right of initiative. Duties: to investigate comprehensively and fully, to give a well-founded and objective conclusion, not to disclose information, and to preserve objects. A knowingly false conclusion entails criminal liability; objectivity and keeping secrecy are mandatory.

t: Responsibility of the expert and recusal
n: Responsibility of the expert and recusal. A person who is legally incapable or of limited capacity cannot be an expert. A person with an unexpunged or unextinguished criminal record also cannot be an expert. The Criminal Code provides Article 238 for a knowingly false conclusion, Article 239 for disclosure of data and Article 240 for evasion of giving a conclusion. Grounds for recusal: kinship, material or official dependence, insufficient qualification. The expert may also recuse himself. Recusal is decided only by the person who ordered the examination: in the inquiry and preliminary investigation within 24 hours, at a court sitting at the same sitting.

t: Specialist and expert: differences
n: Specialist and expert: differences. The specialist, under Article 69 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, helps in finding and securing evidence. He is called in scene inspection and exhumation. His rights: to know the purpose, and to decline if unqualified. Duties: to appear when summoned, and to keep secrecy. The expert, by contrast, is appointed by ruling or court order, establishes and evaluates the medical fact, carries out the investigation and draws up the conclusion. Attention: expert and specialist are not the same thing. The specialist does not draw up an independent document.

t: Procedural types of examination
n: Procedural types of examination. A commission examination is carried out on questions of professional offence, age and health; a complex examination if other sciences are also needed. An additional examination fills a deficiency, usually carried out by the previous expert. A repeat examination is ordered if the conclusion raises doubt. There are five types in all: primary, commission, complex, additional and repeat. Repeat, commission and complex examinations are carried out only in the repeat-commission department of the bureau.

t: Repeat and additional examination: main differences
n: Repeat and additional examination: main differences. Attention: an additional examination is not the same as a repeat examination. An additional examination is ordered to fill a deficiency of the previous conclusion, usually carried out by the previous expert. A repeat examination is ordered if the conclusion is not substantiated or raises doubt, the evidence is unreliable, or the rules were grossly violated; it is usually carried out by 2 or more experts. The original expert cannot carry out a repeat examination; he only gives explanations. Disagreement of the parties alone is not grounds for a repeat examination. Repeat, commission and complex examinations are carried out only in the repeat and commission department of the bureau; they are prohibited in the morphological department and outpatient clinic.

t: The expert's conclusion and the act of examination
n: The expert's conclusion and the act of examination. The expert's conclusion consists of three parts: introduction, investigation and the concluding part, that is, the findings. The findings answer the questions put in clear and comprehensible language that admits no differing interpretation. The basis of the conclusion is a ruling or court order, and the expert is informed of his rights and responsibility. The basis of an act is a written instruction or referral, no receipt is taken, and its final part is the conclusion. The conclusion has no binding evidential force in advance for the court and investigator. If they disagree, this is justified in the ruling or court order.

t: Case analysis 4: procedural document and type of examination
n: Case analysis: procedural document and type of examination. Situation: the conclusion of the primary examination is not substantiated, and there is doubt about its correctness. It has also been established that procedural rules were violated in the previous examination. First question: which examination is ordered, who carries it out and where is it conducted? Second question: one of the parties to the case merely disagrees with the conclusion and gives no other ground. Is a repeat examination ordered? Third question: what must the court do if it disagrees with the new conclusion? Is the conclusion binding on the court?

t: Organisation of the expert service
n: Organisation of the expert service. The main service is in the Ministry of Health; the Ministry of Defence has a separate service for the military. The chain is as follows: Ministry of Health, Chief Bureau, 13 territorial bureaus, district and city units. In administrative and financial matters the territorial bureau is subordinate to the local health authority, and in examination to the Chief Bureau. The composition of the bureau: the morphological department, outpatient clinic, department of repeat and commission examinations, and departments of chemistry, biology and criminalistics.

t: The concept of brain death
n: The concept of brain death. Because organs and tissues differ in phylogenetic age, irreversible changes occur first in the cerebral cortex; CNS integration is disturbed. Death of the cerebral cortex is the beginning of biological death and is accepted as "brain death"; W. Durwald in 1981 called this "individual death". The intermediate period between death of the cortex and death of other organs and tissues is about 20 hours; the removal of organs from a dead body is based on this. Brain death is established in the manner laid down by the Ministry of Health, usually by resuscitation specialists and neurologists.

t: Establishing death: early and reliable signs
n: Establishing death: early and reliable signs. Early signs, even if detected immediately after death, are probable: immobility, pallor of the skin, absence of consciousness, breathing and heartbeat. The earliest reliable sign is the Beloglazov symptom, that is, the "cat's eye"; it is detected after 15–20 minutes. At 1.5–2.0 hours after death the Beloglazov symptom may not be detectable because of rigor of the pupillary muscles. Cooling of the body to 23 degrees and below, cadaveric lividity, rigor and drying are also reliable signs.

t: Supravital reactions and time of death
n: Supravital reactions and time of death. After brain death, in the first period some organs and tissues respond to external action; this is used in determining the time of death. With mechanical action muscles contract for 1–2 hours; up to 10 hours an idiomuscular swelling appears at the site of action, and at 10–11 hours a pit forms. With electric current the muscles of the face, neck, arms and legs contract for 2–3 hours; up to 11–12 hours only the eye muscles. In the first 5–6 hours 1 % atropine dilates the pupil; the reaction of the sweat glands can be tested within 30 hours.

t: Forensic classification of death
n: Forensic classification of death. From the forensic medical standpoint, the category, kind and type of death are distinguished; by category, death is violent or non-violent. Violent death by kind is divided into homicide, suicide and accident; non-violent death is not divided into kinds. Types of violent death: mechanical injury, mechanical asphyxia, poisoning, high and low temperature, electric current. The category and type are determined by the forensic medical expert; determining the kind is within the competence of law-enforcement bodies, because intent is established.

t: Conclusion: main ideas and review questions
n: Conclusion: main ideas and review questions. The service has passed through 4 periods: until the 1920s, until the 1950s, 1950–1991, and from 1991 to the present. An examination is carried out by a ruling of the inquiry or investigation or a court order; in the period of independence the Law "On Forensic Examination" was adopted for the first time. Attention: expert and specialist are not the same thing. The expert gives a conclusion; the specialist helps in finding evidence and does not draw up an independent document. Types of examination: primary, commission, complex, additional and repeat.
